# 2. Data sources and sample description

## 2.1 Data sources and sample construction

We use farm-level microdata from the sixth and seventh rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey (GLSS), fielded in 2012/13 (GLSS6) and 2016/17 (GLSS7) [@GSS2014; @GSS2019]. Both rounds are repeated cross-sections drawn through a two-stage design in which enumeration areas are selected first and households within them second, and they are the only two rounds that administer the household financial-services module in comparable form, which fixes the study window. Farm, household and operator variables come from the consolidated farmer-level GLSS dataset of @Tsiboe2020, which harmonizes the agricultural modules across rounds and has supported a series of analyses of crop production technology and efficiency in Ghana [e.g., @Tsiboe2021a; @Tsiboe2021b; @Adaku2023; @Ansah2023a; @Asravor2024]. The unit of observation is the farm operator, the household member who manages the household's plots. Following the consolidated dataset, we retain crop producers whose yields (kg/ha) fall between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles within each survey round and crop, so that extreme values do not drive the frontier estimates. Each operator contributes one pooled record covering all crops grown, which is the record the frontier analysis uses, and the crop-specific records that underlie the crop rows of Table 1.

Two further restrictions apply upstream of the analysis, and both are complete-case restrictions. First, the harmonized financial module retains operators aged at least eighteen with recorded age, schooling, account-ownership and insurance status, because these items enter the financial-inclusion index and the matching covariates described in Section 4.3, and the index itself is estimated on complete cases of its indicator set. Second, the matching stage of Section 4.3 requires complete information on every matching covariate. The pooled analysis sample, after the first of these restrictions, comprises `r fmt_num(objs$sample$n_pooled, 0)` farm operators, of whom `r fmt_num(objs$treatment$n_treated, 0)` live in households that used credit as defined in Section 2.2 and `r fmt_num(objs$treatment$n_control, 0)` do not (Table 1). Crop output value and planting-material expenditure are expressed per hectare in real terms, as labeled in Table 1. No survey weights are applied, either to the descriptive statistics in Tables 1 to 3 and S1 to S2 or to the estimation; the statistics therefore describe the surveyed crop producers rather than population totals, although the GLSS is designed to be representative at the national and regional levels.

## 2.2 Measuring credit use and the other financial-service indicators

The consolidated dataset does not carry the financial-services module, so the credit and financial-service indicators are rebuilt from Part B, Section 12a of the original GLSS questionnaires and merged to the farmer-level file; Table S0 documents the source items and their mapping. An individual is a credit user if, in the twelve months preceding the interview, the person applied for a loan, the application was granted and a positive loan amount was recorded; a person who applied and was refused, or whose application was still pending, is a non-user. Note S2 sets out the construction, the differences between the two rounds' instruments and what the indicator measures: it records the use of credit rather than access to it, counts a loan from any source and for any purpose, and uses a twelve-month recall window that is not tied to the cropping calendar, so it should be read as household credit use rather than as agricultural credit.

Our preferred treatment is defined at the household level: a farm operator is a credit user if the operator, the operator's spouse, a child of the operator, or any other household member satisfies the individual criterion. Aggregating to the household reflects the pooling of liquidity within farm households. A loan taken by a spouse relaxes the same cash constraint on the same farm, and the technology the frontier analysis characterizes is the household's, not the operator's borrowing record. By this definition `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$share_hh, 1)` of operators live in a household that used credit. The operator personally satisfied the criterion in `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$share_hh - objs$credit$reclass_farmer_only, 1)` of the sample, so that in about `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$reclass_farmer_only / objs$credit$share_hh, 0)` of credit-using households the loan was held by a spouse, a child or another member rather than by the operator; the household categories overlap, since a household may contain more than one borrower, and Table S1 reports the number of operators in each. The farmer-only variant, which counts only the operator's own borrowing, is a strict subset of the household measure, because no operator borrows in a household recorded as having no credit, and it reclassifies `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$reclass_farmer_only, 1)` of the sample from user to non-user. Unless stated otherwise, "credit user" refers to the household measure. Section 5 reports the frontier comparison under the household definition and under the operator-only, spouse and other-member definitions (Table 5), and Tables S1 and S2 describe the characteristics and trends of the corresponding subsamples.

## 2.3 Production variables

The frontier analysis of Section 4 uses the real value of crop output as the dependent variable and six inputs: cultivated land, planting material, family labor, hired labor, fertilizer and pesticide. Table 1 reports these in the units in which they are summarized, namely real GH₵ per hectare for output and planting material, adult equivalents for family labor, man-days per hectare for hired labor, kilograms per hectare for fertilizer and liters per hectare for pesticide, together with indicators for the use of mechanized equipment and irrigation. The determinants of inefficiency (Table S4) and the characteristics on which credit users and non-users are matched are set out where each specification is defined, in Sections 4.2 and 4.3. Table S5 in the appendix defines every variable entering the frontier, the inefficiency term and the matching distance, states the unit in which it is measured, and gives the sign expected of it where theory or the Ghanaian evidence implies one.

## 2.4 Descriptive statistics

Table 1 summarizes the farmer, production and household characteristics of the pooled sample and of credit users and non-users, together with the annual percentage change in each characteristic between the two rounds; daggers mark characteristics on which users and non-users differ at the 5% level. Credit users are younger and markedly more educated than non-users, less likely to own the land they farm and more reliant on hired labor, while output value per hectare does not differ significantly between the groups. Note S3 describes the crops grown, the sample as a whole, the contrasts between users and non-users, the trends between rounds and the profile of borrowing households by who holds the loan (Table S1).

The descriptive evidence carries two implications for the empirical strategy. First, credit users differ from non-users in age, schooling, tenure and hired labor, characteristics that also predict technology choice and technical efficiency, and their composition shifts between rounds, so an unconditional comparison of frontier outcomes would confound the association with credit with differences in who borrows; the pool of non-users is large, with about `r fmt_num(objs$treatment$n_control / objs$treatment$n_treated, 0)` non-users per user, so a close counterpart for each borrower is available. Second, whether borrowing and non-borrowing households operate the same production technology cannot be settled from sample means, and the financing environment described in the next section gives reason to doubt it. Whether credit-using households in fact operate closer to or farther from the best-practice frontier is the empirical question the remainder of the paper addresses.
